prompt: Explain cryptocurrency using only county-fair carnival-game metaphors. The rigged ones.
response:
# Cryptocurrency: A Rigged Carnival Guide

## The Ring Toss (Mining)
See those bottles the rings never quite fit over? That's mining. The barker says "anyone can win!"—technically true. But the rings are sized *just* wrong, and the guy who runs the booth has custom rings that fit perfectly. Early miners got the good rings. You get the wobbly ones and a $3,000 electric bill.

## The Milk Bottle Throw (Volatility)
The bottles are weighted at the bottom with lead. You *can* knock them down, but only if you throw with divine force at exactly the right angle at exactly the right moment. Miss that window and you've spent your rent money learning the bottles were never meant to fall for you.

## The "Everyone's a Winner" Claw Machine (Altcoins)
The claw has precisely calibrated grip strength—strong enough to lift the prize halfway, weak enough to drop it every time. New coins launch with a claw that grips *beautifully* for the founders' first few grabs, then mysteriously loosens right when the crowd arrives.

## The Balloon Dart Game (Pump and Dump)
"Pop any balloon, win big!" The barker's friends keep winning huge prizes in front of you—see how easy it is? What you don't see: those balloons are barely inflated for insiders. Yours are made of tire rubber. By the time you're throwing, everyone who won already left with the good stuff.

## The Guy Who Holds Your Prize (Exchanges)
"I'll keep your giant teddy bear at the booth so you can keep playing!" You come back at the end of the night. The booth is gone. The teddy bear is gone. There is a sign that reads *"Not Your Booth, Not Your Bear."*

## The Cotton Candy (The Whitepaper)
Looks enormous and substantial. Costs a fortune. Dissolves into nothing the moment you actually try to consume it.

---

*Prize redemption not guaranteed. Barker not liable. The house always wins—that's the whole innovation.*
